title.value: Protein posttranslational modifications of Giardia histones

projectDescription.value: Diarrheal disease caused by Giardia duodenalis is highly prevalent, totalling over 200 million cases globally each year. The processes which drive parasite virulence, host immune evasion and transmission involve coordinated gene expression, which are likely post-transcriptionally regulated. Epigenetic regulatory systems are eukaryote-conserved, including in deep-branching excavates such as Giardia, with several studies already implicating histone post-translational modifications (PTMs) in regulation of its pathogenesis and life cycle. However, further insights into Giardia chromatin dynamics have been hindered by a lack of site-specific data. Using mass spectrometry, we have provided the first molecular map of histone methylation, acetylation and phosphorylation modifications in Giardia core histones. We have identified over 50 previously unreported histone modifications, including recognised epigenetic sites, combinatorial modifications indicative of PTM crosstalk, and co-occurring modifications previously correlated in model eukaryotes. These demonstrate a conserved histone code in Giardia that is equivalent to many other eukaryotes, and suggest that similar epigenetic mechanisms are in place in this parasite. Further, we used sequence, domain and structural homology to annotate putative histone enzyme networks in Giardia, highlighting representative chromatin modifiers which appear sufficient for identified sites, particularly those from H3 and H4 variants. This study is the first and most comprehensive, complete and accurate view of Giardia histone PTMs to date, and a substantial step towards understanding their associations in parasite development and virulence.

sampleProcessingProtocol.value: Cultures of Giardia duodenalis WB isolate (WB-1B (Upcroft et al., 1995) were maintained in flat-sided tubes (Nuclon) in complete TYI-S33 containing 10% bovine serum and 0.5g/L bovine bile. Larger cell volume pellets (~250uL cellvolume) were obtained by scaling up cultures in upright and stationary in custom borosilicate glass 500mL “outside-in” roller-bottles as previously described (Emery-Corbin et al., 2018). Biological triplicate cell pellets were lysed to enrich for a nuclear pellet as previously described (Yee and Joseph, 2011) followed by acid extraction to enrich for histone proteins (Shechter et al., 2007). The histone enriched fraction underwent acetone precipitation, was quantified for protein concentration via by bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay (Pierce), and separated via gel electrophoresis on a Novex® 16%, Tris-Glycine (Invitrogen). Each biological triplicate was run as 3 technical replicates for multi-protease digestion with Trypsin, ASP-N and ARG-C (Giansanti et al., 2016).   Low molecular weight protein bands corresponding histones were excised and subjected to in-gel digestion and peptide extraction as previously described (Neilson et al., 2014), with ARG-C digestion conditions in 150 mM ammonium bicarbonate, 15 mM CaCl2, 10 mM DTT and ASP-N digestion in 25 mM ammonium bicarbonate with 0.15 μg of each protease added to each gel band. After peptide extraction samples were desalted us in-house C18 stage tips are previously described (Rappsilber et al., 2007), vacuum centrifuged to dryness (as above), and peptides dissolved in 0.1% TFA and 2% ACN for LC-MS/MS.   LC-MS/MS analysis of in-gel digested histone bands were performed on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos (Thermo) at the Bio21 mass spectrometry facility (University of Melbourne). Chromatographic separation of peptide mixtures took place on an interfaced nano-LC system (Ultimate 3000 RSLC, Dionex) equipped with an Acclaim Pepmap nano-trap column (Dionex – C18, 100 Å, 75 μm × 2 cm) and an Acclaim Pepmap RSLC analytical column (Dionex – C18, 100 Å, 75 μm × 50 cm) kept at 50°C. Each sample was analysed on a 45min gradient ranging 3%-85% ACN in 0.1% formic acid (FA) at 300nL/minute. Eluting peptides were ionized using positive ion mode nano-ESI with 240,000 resolution scanning from 400-1500 m/z in full scan with lockmass of 401.92272. Data dependent MS2 was carried out using the 3 second maximum cycle method. MS2 was carried out in HCD mode with resolution of 15,000, normalized collision energy of 35%, AGC target of 50000 and Activation Q of 0.25 for ions above 50,000. Former target ions selected for MS/MS were dynamically excluded for 45 s.

dataProcessingProtocol.value: Maxquant (Tyanova et al., 2016) software (v1.5.8.3) was used for database searching with the Assemblage A WB genome (ATCC 50803, release 34) from GiardiaDB.org (Aurrecoechea et al., 2009) along with sequences containing common contaminants. Three searches were performed with respective protease parameters (Trypsin, ASP-N, AR-C) parameters for each of the three sets of MS/MS raw files obtained from LC-MS/MS corresponding to each digestion (total 15 files for each protease). Each search included additional parameters of maximum 2 missed cleavages, carbamidomethylation as a fixed modification, peptide length of minimum 7 amino acids, and peptide and protein false discovery rate set to 0.01. Variable modifications included protein N-terminal acetylation, methionine oxidation, lysine/arginine monomethylation, lysine demethylation, lysine trimethylation, lysine acetylation and serine/threonine/tyrosine phosphorylation as variable modifications.  MaxQuant output tables (“msms.txt”, “peptides.txt”, and site tables for “Acetyl (K)Sites.txt”, “Methyl (K/R)Sites.txt”, “Dimethyl (K)Sites.txt” and “Trimethyl (K)Sites.txt”, and “Phospho (STY)Sites.txt”) were processed by means of adapting a custom R script (available at https://github.com/JoshuaHamey/MethylSite-Filtering). This script was used to create modification-specific MS/MS tables for all variable modifications (N-term Ac, KAc, K/RMMe, KDMe, KTMe, S/T/YPh) for each of the three proteases, as well as combined PTM site tables. Sites were filtered by 3 different sets of criteria, producing 3 filtered site tables. Firstly, sites underwent general confidence filteing (Score ≥ 60, Calculated “true” Delta Score ≥ 10, Localisation ≥ .90, Peptide length ≤ 100), and only sites that met these cutoffs were reported. A second site table for higher confidence sites was also generated (Score ≥ 80, Calculated “true” Delta Score ≥ 20, Localisation ≥ .95, Peptide length ≤ 30, Unique Peptides ≥ 2), to indicate sites with most robust evidence. Lastly, sites were filtered solely for MS/MS data which indicated detection of 1 adjacent site fragment ion before and after the reported modification site (=2/4 fragment ions). Filtered methylation sites were specifically checked to have met fragment-ion filtering, and only filtered methylation sites which also had adjacent site ions were reported.
